items.title: New model measures full economic value of accurate hurricane forecasts
items.summary: When it comes to the cost of a bad forecast, researchers have gone beyond damaged buildings and vehicles to calculate the cost of injuries, evacuations and the long-term loss of public trust.

items.title: Is bird flu infecting humans? How would we know?
items.summary: Bird flu is circulating among birds on the Australian mainland. So, with the confirmed number of detections growing, you may be wondering about the risk of birds infecting humans.

items.title: The brightened night sky nobody actually wanted
items.summary: A new paper has put hard numbers on a plan that's been rattling around the astronomy community for a while now—a California company called Reflect Orbital wants to put giant mirrors in orbit and beam sunlight down to Earth after dark. items.title: Amber fossil reveals firefly relative with unprecedented antennae
items.summary: Insects rely on a wide range of strategies to sense their surroundings and communicate with their peers. Fireflies (Lampyridae) and some related beetles are known for their ability to produce visible light through chemical reactions that take place in specialized light-producing organs.

items.title: Can dogs help teens cope with peer stress?
items.summary: About one in 10 teenagers experiences social anxiety—persistent and disruptive worries about being judged by classmates and other peers. items.title: The Nigerian fishing community being eaten up by the Atlantic
items.summary: The beach shrinks every year in Ayetoro, in southern Nigeria, and what is left is peppered with the remains of homes swallowed by the ocean—some years ago, some just months prior.

items.title: Hawaii recovery efforts begin as Lala is downgraded, moves west
items.summary: Clean-up efforts were underway Sunday as Hurricane Lala, which was downgraded to a tropical storm, rolled past Hawaii's Big Island and dumped heavy rain across the U.S. Pacific state.

items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected
items.summary: An eight-year Finnish study found that children who spent more time on screens tended to show better cognitive processing as teenagers, challenging common assumptions about screen use. Researchers say the key may be balancing physical activity with screen activities that encourage learning, creativi

items.title: Animals have been eating nature’s original bioplastic for millions of years
items.summary: Nature invented biodegradable plastic long before humans did—and animals may have been feeding on it for hundreds of millions of years. items.title: Tiny graphene wrinkles create surprisingly powerful electrical effects
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that tiny, sharply curved wrinkles in graphene can dramatically alter its electrical behavior, creating surprisingly strong charge separation. items.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
items.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to comba

items.title: Giant crocodylians dominated the food chain in Miocene South America, fossil evidence suggests
items.summary: South America was a frightening place during the Miocene. More than 10 million years ago, a vast lake covered much of the continent, home to giant turtles and crocodylians.

items.title: Flightless beetles evolved distinct snail-hunting shapes on Japan's largest island
items.summary: Islands are widely recognized as natural laboratories of evolution. The ocean restricts movement among islands, allowing isolated populations to adapt to different environments and, at times, diverge into new species. However, on large islands, geographic distance may restrict movement, while enviro

items.title: Radio telescopes help scientists map molecules in space and uncover where and how stars form
items.summary: You may have heard the phrase "we are made of star-stuff." This statement by the astronomer Carl Sagan refers to the fact that elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were forged in the centers of the first stars. But how does this star-stuff evolve into the chemistry of rocks, plants and people?

items.title: Brief firearm safety talks more than double openness to out-of-home storage
items.summary: A brief chat about firearm safety can sharply increase willingness among gun owners to consider temporarily storing their firearms outside the home during times of crisis, a step that could help reduce suicide risk, according to a Rutgers-led study.

items.title: Hurricane Lala pulls away from Hawaii's Big Island
items.summary: Hurricane Lala was pulling away from Hawaii's Big Island early Sunday as heavy rain and strong winds struck the U.S. Pacific state and officials warned of potentially dangerous flooding.

items.title: Belgium races to tame huge wildfire creeping toward Germany
items.summary: Water-bombing aircraft and farmers' tractors joined forces Sunday to help firefighters tame Belgium's largest modern-day wildfire, which has scorched vast swaths of a hard-to-reach nature reserve near the German border.

items.title: Japan aims for the moons of Mars
items.summary: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars' moons to retrieve samples that may unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, although a rival Chinese mission aims to make it back first.

items.title: A small squeeze reveals new clues about an unusual kind of magnet
items.summary: Researchers at Rice University have found that gently squeezing a crystal of iron sulfide can change two of its unusual properties at the same time: its tiny magnetic signal and the way electricity moves through it. The result gives scientists a clearer picture of how a newly recognized class of mag

items.title: Gene-edited beagles produce no detectable major dog allergen, early tests find
items.summary: Humans love dogs, but petting them can leave some people sneezing and wheezing. About 15% of the world's population lives with a dog allergy, which can increase the risk of hay fever and asthma. The main culprit is Can f 1, a protein found mainly in dog saliva. items.title: Phytophthora dieback linked to habitat loss and lower digging activity among quendas in Western Australia
items.summary: A new study from Murdoch University has found that the introduced plant disease Phytophthora dieback is indirectly hindering quendas in Western Australia's jarrah forests by reducing their habitat quality and consequently decreasing their digging activity. items.title: Strain flips Hall signal in altermagnetic manganese telluride, suggesting a path to practical spintronics
items.summary: Time-reversal symmetry is an exotic behavior found in systems whose internal physics looks different when running forward versus backward in time. items.title: Chinese ship sets off for Europe through Arctic, halving travel time
items.summary: A Chinese container vessel has set sail for Europe through the Arctic as part of a new weekly service on a route that cuts shipment times in half but that environmental groups warn could speed up the melting of polar ice.

items.title: Firefighters battle second day of blaze on Greek island
items.summary: Firefighters battled for a second day Sunday to contain a forest fire on the Greek Aegean island of Skyros, as the local mayor voiced hope it could soon be brought under control.

items.title: Shrinking water bodies can turn drought into disease hotspots or dead ends
items.summary: Prolonged dry spells or droughts can sometimes reduce aquatic diseases, many of which affect people. Yet other times, water scarcity can counterintuitively lead to an uptick in diseases that depend on water.

items.title: Einstein Probe catches rare X-ray flash from an exploding star
items.summary: Astronomers have linked an X-ray flash discovered by the Einstein Probe to a known type of supernova with unusual features that point to the birth of an ultra-dense, rapidly spinning magnetar. The paper outlining this finding was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on July 22.

items.title: Active particles could make stable glasses stronger without catastrophic brittle failure
items.summary: The strongest glasses have an Achilles' heel that causes them to fail catastrophically when pushed past their limit. items.title: This 10-cent heart drug cuts hospitalizations by 25%
items.summary: A centuries-old heart drug costing less than ten cents a day could help keep heart-failure patients out of the hospital. New research suggests low-dose digoxin can reduce heart-failure hospitalizations by about 25%, potentially paving the way for its return as a major treatment.

items.title: Why AI training can backfire for older workers
items.summary: Employers are increasingly investing in training to prepare their employees for artificial intelligence (AI). Training budgets are growing, and "upskilling" has become a common response to rapid technological change.
